obs_text: The characteristic is named from ἀργός (idle/ineffective/careless), part of the M67 diligence-vs-negligence cluster. The name signals absence of productive activity -- the negation of engaged effort, whether physical (idleness), verbal (careless speech), or spiritual (fruitlessness).

ἀργός is a compound (privative ἀ- + ἔργον, 'work'), literally 'without work'. LSJ shows the base agricultural sense 'not working the ground', extended to 'idle, lazy' (opposed to ἐργάτις) and, of things, 'lying idle, yielding no return' (of money), 'fallow' (of land), 'unwrought'. Mounce/tree converge on idle/lazy/useless/ineffective/careless.

The a-privative + ἔργον construction carries a constitutional implication: the word defines its subject negatively, by the absence of expected productive output, rather than by any positive quality. This makes it naturally paired with fruit/growth imagery (2 Pet 1:8's ἄκαρπος) and with accounting language (Matt 12:36's λόγος/account for careless words).

Primary Greek term ἀργός, from ἀ- (privative) + ἔργον ('work, deed'). Root meaning: 'not-working', hence idle, unproductive, ineffective. No Hebrew equivalent is in view for this NT-only term in this cluster's data.

ἀργός is an adjective (attested only as A- morph forms across the given occurrences: A-APM, A-ASN, A-NPM), modifying persons (idle laborers, Matt 20:6), words (careless speech, Matt 12:36), and qualities/character (ineffective in knowledge, 2 Pet 1:8). Its purely adjectival range shows the characteristic operates as a descriptor of state/condition rather than as an act in itself.

Semantic range spans: (1) literal physical idleness/unemployment (Matt 20:6, standing idle in the marketplace), (2) morally-loaded 'careless' speech implying culpable inattention rather than mere inactivity (Matt 12:36), (3) metaphorical spiritual unfruitfulness/ineffectiveness paired with ἄκαρπος (2 Pet 1:8). LSJ also documents financial idleness (money 'lying idle, yielding no return') and agricultural fallowness, showing the term's economic/productivity register carried into its NT moral use.
The structural opposite within this cluster's own vocabulary is σπουδή/σπουδαίως (G4710/G4709), denoting earnestness, zeal, diligent effort -- the positive filling of the void ἀργός names.

None. No supplication/seeking term for idleness/diligence appears among ἀργός's own occurrences; the cluster's positive counterpart σπουδή is described as an inward quality/exertion, not something requested from another.

As this is an NT-only term in these occurrences without an OT Hebrew counterpart supplied, the vocabulary shows a purely Greek moral-philosophical development: classical Greek used ἀργός mainly for physical/economic idleness (fallow land, unworked money), while its NT use extends the term to moral and spiritual unfruitfulness (careless words, ineffective faith), a semantic broadening rather than displacement.
None. ἀργός is a well-attested classical Greek term (from Homer onward per LSJ), not a NT-period coinage; its NT usage develops existing sense rather than introducing a new word.

The full arc runs from concrete physical/economic non-work (fallow land, idle money, unemployed persons standing in the marketplace) through morally-charged idle speech (careless words that will be judged) to a metaphorical extension describing spiritual unproductiveness (ineffective/unfruitful in the knowledge of Christ). The range consistently centers on absence of expected productive output across physical, verbal, and spiritual domains.

In 2Pet.1.8 ἀργός shifts from its base 'idle/unemployed' gloss to a metaphorical 'ineffective' sense applied to spiritual qualities, paired with ἄκαρπος ('unfruitful') -- the nuance here is qualitative barrenness of Christian character rather than literal non-labor. In Matt.12.36 the shift is toward 'careless/thoughtless' applied to speech -- not mere silence but reckless, unweighed utterance that incurs judgment, a moral-culpability nuance absent from the base 'idle' sense. In Matt.20.6 the term sits squarely within its base literal sense (physically standing idle, unemployed) with no notable shift.

In 2Pet.1.8, ἀργός/ἄκαρπος (M67) modifies the state of the believer's relation to M15 (knowledge/ἐπίγνωσις) -- the diligence-cluster term functions as the negative condition that increasing virtues (qualities named in v.5-7) are said to prevent, making M67 the hinge describing failure-mode outcome relative to M15's positive content.

σπουδή derives from σπεύδω ('to hasten'). LSJ shows the primary sense as physical 'haste, speed', extending to 'zeal, pains, trouble, effort' and 'earnestness' as a serious, engaged disposition contrasted with playfulness (παιδιά). Mounce/tree agree: haste, diligence, enthusiasm, zeal.

σπουδή occurs here only as a noun (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-ASF, N-DSF across occurrences), naming a quality or state rather than the act itself; the related adverb σπουδαίως (G4709) supplies the manner-of-action form, showing the characteristic operates both as a describable quality possessed and as a manner in which action is carried out.

Semantic range spans literal physical haste/speed (Mark 6:25, 'with haste' to the king), zeal as attentive/earnest effort in relationships and undertakings (Rom 12:11, 'not lagging in zeal'), and a demonstrable, quasi-evidentiary sense -- earnestness that others can observe and that functions as proof of genuine character (2 Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8, where σπουδή is offered as evidence of repentance and love alongside other virtues).

The structural opposites within this cluster's own vocabulary are ἀργός (G0692, idle/ineffective) and ὀκνηρός (G3636, slothful/reluctant) -- both name the deficiency or absence that σπουδή positively fills.

The full arc moves from concrete physical haste/speed, through general zealous exertion and attentiveness (including political/partisan zeal in classical usage), to an ethical-relational sense in the NT epistles where earnestness becomes visible proof of sincere character (repentance, love, generosity) offered for others to observe and judge.

In Mark.6.25 σπουδή retains its base literal sense of physical haste ('with haste' to the king) with no metaphorical shift. In 2Cor.7.11, 7.12, 8.7, 8.8 and Rom.12.11 the term shifts from physical speed to an ethical-relational nuance of demonstrable zeal/earnestness functioning as evidence of sincerity -- a marked shift from the base 'haste' gloss toward a virtue-term describing wholehearted moral engagement, distinctive to the Pauline corpus's use compared to the narrative/literal use in Mark.

In Rom.12.11, σπουδή/ζέω (M67 zeal + M69 fervent) stand together with M47 (spirit/πνεῦμα) and M78 (serve/δουλεύω), with ὀκνηρός (M67, slothful) as the negative to be avoided -- M67's own vantage adds that this is a triad of intensifiers (not lagging, being fervent, serving the Lord) where zeal is the connective quality binding inward fervor of spirit to outward service.

The adverbial form of the M67 cluster, from σπουδαῖος, naming the manner of acting 'earnestly, promptly' -- signaling that an action is performed with the wholehearted urgency at the core of this cluster's positive pole.

σπουδαίως relates to σπουδή/σπουδαῖος (from σπεύδω, 'hasten'). LSJ documents the base sense as 'in haste, quick', extended to 'with energy or earnestness', 'seriously', 'zealously, in the best way'. Mounce/tree give simply 'earnestly, promptly'.

As an adverb, the word carries a manner-implication: it modifies the intensity/urgency with which an action toward another party is undertaken -- here qualifying the intercessory pleading of the elders on the centurion's behalf.
Primary Greek term σπουδαίως (adverb of σπουδαῖος, from σπουδή/σπεύδω). Root meaning: urgently, with serious energy. No Hebrew counterpart is in view for this NT-only occurrence.

σπουδαίως is exclusively an adverb (ADV morph code), showing this cluster-member operates purely as a manner-qualifier of a verb (here παρακαλέω, 'to plead'), never as a noun or adjective in this occurrence -- underscoring that the characteristic here describes HOW an action is carried out rather than naming a possessed quality.

Semantic range narrows to manner-of-action: from base 'in haste, quick' (of physical movement) to 'seriously, zealously, with energy' when applied to human effort or entreaty -- in Luke 7:4 specifically intensifying an act of intercessory pleading, showing the range extends from physical urgency to relational/moral intensity of advocacy.
Within the cluster, this adverb (manner-of-act) is distinguished from σπουδή (G4710, the noun naming the disposition/quality of zeal itself) -- i.e., act-modifier versus disposition-noun.

The structural opposite within the cluster is ὀκνηρῶς (implied adverb of ὀκνηρός, G3636, 'reluctantly/sluggishly'), though not itself among these occurrences; ἀργός (G0692) supplies the adjectival opposite of idle/ineffective action.
None. No person-type term is attested for this adverb; it modifies action rather than naming an agent-type.

No separate seeking-term for the characteristic itself; rather, in this very verse σπουδαίως modifies παρακαλέω (G3870, 'to beg/plead'), the general supplication-verb -- the earnestness intensifies an entreaty act performed by others, not a request FOR earnestness.

No Hebrew equivalent supplied; the adverb's classical Greek development (LSJ) moves from a purely physical sense ('in haste, quick') toward a moral-qualitative sense ('earnest, serious, good/excellent of its kind'), a broadening that the single NT occurrence draws on for its intensified pleading.
None. σπουδαίως derives from the long-attested classical adjective σπουδαῖος (Herodotus onward); not an NT-period coinage.

The arc runs from purely physical 'in haste, quick' (of feet, of pace) to a moral-qualitative sense of 'good, excellent, serious' applied to persons and their pursuits in classical usage, narrowing in its single NT occurrence to intensify an act of earnest intercessory pleading on another's behalf.

The base gloss for σπουδαίως is 'earnestly, promptly', but in Luke 7:4 the nuance carried is specifically intensified relational advocacy -- the Jewish elders plead 'earnestly' meaning insistently and with full personal investment on behalf of a third party (the centurion), rather than simple speed or promptness of the pleading act itself. This is the sole NT occurrence, so no comparison across other instances is possible.

The verse's operation word is παρακαλέω ('pleaded', T3-tagged in role list), initiated by the elders (subject, implicit party) and directed toward Jesus (accusative object, party present, T7/T8-tagged) on behalf of the centurion. σπουδαίως (M67, T2) intensifies the manner of this operation but is not itself the T3-tagged operation word.

No other M-code characteristic is present in Luke.7.4's role list; σπουδαίως (M67) stands alone here, intensifying the pleading (παρακαλέω) directed at Jesus concerning the centurion's worthiness (ἄξιος, itself not M-tagged in this list).

The characteristic named from ὀκνηρός ('slothful, hesitant, timid') is the disposition-pole of the M67 cluster, signaling a shrinking-back or reluctance rooted in timidity/fear rather than mere inactivity.

ὀκνηρός derives from ὄκνος ('hesitation, shrinking, fear'). LSJ's core sense is 'shrinking, timid', especially from fear, opposed to τολμηρός ('bold'); secondarily 'idle, sluggish'. Mounce/tree give 'lazy, idle, not active; troublesome'.

The word carries a relational/directional implication toward action or engagement that is being avoided or shrunk from -- LSJ's 'causing fear, vexatious, troublesome' sense (of things) shows the term can describe not only the timid person but the burdensome task from which one shrinks.
Primary Greek term ὀκνηρός, from ὄκνος ('hesitation/timidity/fear'). Root meaning: shrinking back from fear, hence reluctant, sluggish, slothful. No Hebrew equivalent supplied for this NT-only term.

ὀκνηρός is an adjective (A-NPM in this occurrence), modifying persons directly ('be not slothful [ones]'), showing the characteristic operates as a state/disposition ascribed to a person rather than an isolated act.

Semantic range spans fear-rooted timidity/hesitation before action (LSJ's primary sense, opposed to τολμηρός 'bold'), general idleness/sluggishness, and (of things) 'vexatious, troublesome' -- describing what causes reluctance as well as the reluctant disposition itself.

Distinguishes disposition (ὀκνηρός: fear-rooted reluctance/timidity as an inner shrinking) from mere state of inactivity (ἀργός, G0692: idle without necessarily implying fear as the cause) within the same M67 cluster.

The structural opposite is τολμηρός ('bold, daring'), explicitly named by LSJ as the antonym to ὀκνηρός, though τολμηρός is not itself among this cluster's supplied strongs. Within the cluster, σπουδή/G4710 (zeal) supplies the positive counter-quality the exhortation urges instead of ὀκνηρός.
None distinct within this occurrence; ὀκνηρός itself functions substantivally when applied directly to persons, but no separate agent-noun form is attested here.
None. No supplication/seeking term for overcoming sloth is present among these occurrences; the exhortation is a direct imperative ('do not be...') rather than a petition.

No Hebrew counterpart supplied; the term's development is intra-Greek, moving from a fear-rooted psychological/military sense in classical usage (soldiers 'more timid' in battle, LSJ) to a general moral exhortation against sluggishness in the Christian life in its sole NT occurrence.
None. ὀκνηρός is attested from classical sources (Pindar, Xenophon, Demosthenes per LSJ), not coined in the NT period.

The full arc runs from military/psychological timidity (shrinking from danger, opposed to boldness) through general idleness/sluggishness to, in its single NT occurrence, a moral exhortation against spiritual/relational sloth as the opposite pole to the zeal (ζῆλος) commanded in the same verse.

In Rom.12.11 ὀκνηρός sits within its base gloss ('slothful, indolent') with no notable surface divergence -- the exhortation 'do not be slothful in zeal' uses the term in its standard moral-ethical sense as attested elsewhere (e.g. Matt 25:26), so no shift is recorded.

In Rom.12.11, ὀκνηρός (M67) stands paired with σπουδή/M67's own zeal-term and alongside M69 (fervent/ζέω), M47 (spirit/πνεῦμα), and M78 (serve/δουλεύω) -- M67's own vantage adds that the negated disposition (not being slothful) is the necessary precondition cleared before the positive triad of zeal, fervor of spirit, and service to the Lord can be enacted; the verse structures M67 as both negative prohibition and positive command in a single breath.

Greek spoudē at the definitional level denotes 'haste, speed,' extending to 'zeal, pains, effort, earnestness' and even 'esteem, regard' for a person — showing the term bridges swift physical motion and sustained moral/relational diligence.

Grammatical range is nominal (N-DSF/N-ASF), functioning as the object of prepositions ('with zeal', 'with haste') or as direct object of verbs ('show earnestness'), showing the characteristic operates as a quality or manner brought to bear on an action rather than an action itself.

The vocabulary arc for spoudē runs from physical haste/speed, through effortful diligence and zealous exertion in tasks, to personal esteem/regard, religious zeal, and full assurance of hope — showing the term's capacity to describe both the manner of action and the intensity of relational/spiritual commitment across these three occurrences (leadership, writing urgency, and hope-related diligence).

In Jude 1:3 the surface rendering 'eager' shifts spoudē from its more common 'zeal/earnestness-as-manner' sense (as in Rom 12:8, Heb 6:11) toward describing an author's personal urgent desire/intention to write - the nuance here is anticipatory eagerness redirected ('although I was very eager... I found it necessary instead'), showing the term can denote a thwarted or redirected intention rather than sustained active diligence, distinguishing this occurrence from the steady diligence sense elsewhere.

The operation word 'write' (G1125, role-T3) is the object of the eagerness (G4710); the author (a party, 'I') initiates the intended act of writing directed toward 'you' (the recipients, a party) concerning their common salvation.

No prior context recorded. From eagerness's own vantage: this verse pairs the author's eagerness with M79 (salvation) as its intended topic and M44 (contend) and M13 (faith) as the redirected actual purpose - eagerness here functions as the initial impulse that is redirected into the necessity of defending the faith, showing a contrast between intended and actual epistolary purpose.
The characteristic is named okneros, 'slothful, reluctant, shrinking.' The name signals timid hesitation and avoidance of exertion, rooted in fear or reluctance rather than mere inactivity.

Greek okneros at the definitional level denotes 'shrinking, timid,' especially from fear, opposed to tolmeros ('bold'); by extension it denotes idle, sluggish persons, and of things, 'causing fear, vexatious, troublesome.'

The name carries a relational implication: sloth is fundamentally a failure of responsive action toward an entrusted task or person (the servant's sloth is measured against the master's expectation) — it names a relational deficiency, not merely private inertia.

Primary Greek term okneros derives from the root sense of shrinking back or hesitating (related to oknos, 'hesitation, reluctance'); its root meaning is fundamentally about fear-driven avoidance of action rather than simple absence of activity. No Hebrew term supplied in these sources.

Grammatical range is adjectival (A-VSM/A-NSN), applied to persons (a slothful servant) and to things/situations (no trouble/burden) — showing the characteristic operates both as a moral descriptor of persons and as a descriptor of a burdensome state of affairs.

Semantic range spans timid reluctance/hesitancy (of persons shrinking from action, especially from fear) to, of things, 'troublesome, vexatious' - an idiomatic shift from subjective disposition (fearful hesitancy) to an objective quality (causing trouble to others), as seen in the contrast between Matt 25:26 (the servant himself is slothful) and Phil 3:1 (writing the same things is 'no trouble/okneron' to Paul).

The vocabulary distinguishes disposition (a slothful/timid character, Matt 25:26) from a resulting quality of a task or act (troublesome/burdensome, Phil 3:1) - the same word covers both the inner reluctance and its outward effect.

The structural opposite given directly in LSJ is tolmeros ('bold, daring') - okneros is explicitly defined as opposed to tolmeros. Within this cluster, spoudaios/spoudē (earnest zeal) also function as opposites in effect.
The adjective itself used substantivally supplies the person-type sense: 'the slothful/timid one' (ho okneros), as applied directly to the servant in Matt 25:26 ('you wicked and slothful servant').
None - no supplication/seeking term for slothfulness is supplied; it is a censured condition, not something sought.

No Hebrew term is supplied in these sources; continuity is intra-Greek, moving from classical usage (fearful hesitancy, opposed to boldness) directly into the Gospel parable's moral censure of a servant's failure to act.
None - okneros is attested in classical Greek from the 5th century BC onward, not a NT-period coinage.

The vocabulary arc for okneros runs from fearful/timid hesitation to shrink from action (of persons), through idle sluggishness, to a further sense (of things) as 'troublesome, vexatious' - showing the term's ability to shift from describing an inner reluctant disposition to describing an external burdensome quality, spanning both NT occurrences here.

In Phil 3:1 the surface gloss 'trouble' diverges markedly from the base gloss 'slothful/lazy' used of persons in Matt 25:26. Here the nuance shifts entirely from a moral character-flaw (reluctant, timid inactivity) to a neutral-to-mild sense of 'burdensome/tedious' applied to the act of repeating instruction. The impact is that Paul reframes what could seem an unwelcome repetition as actually 'no trouble' - a litotes downplaying any negative connotation. This is a clear divergence from the censorious personal usage seen in the Matthew parable.

The operation word 'know' (G1492I, role-T3) is directed by the master (a party, 'his master') toward the servant (a party, 'you wicked and slothful servant') as a rhetorical accusation: the master initiates the charge of knowing (or failing to act on known expectations) against the servant characterized as slothful.

No prior context recorded. From sloth's own vantage: this verse pairs slothfulness with M58 (wicked, ponēros) as twin epithets applied by the master to the servant (M78) - sloth here functions as the specific charge of inactivity that, alongside wickedness, together constitute the master's condemnation; sloth is thus one half of a dual accusation rather than standing alone.

The operation word 'write' (G1125, role-T3) is present and directed by Paul (a party, 'my') toward 'you' (the Philippians, a party), but the 'trouble' term (G3636) itself functions as a predicate describing writing's quality, not as the initiator or recipient of a separate operation.

No prior context recorded. From this characteristic's vantage: 'trouble' (G3636) here is paired with M19 (safe, asphales) as a positive complement - repeating instruction is framed as no burden (G3636) and as a safeguard (M19) for the readers, showing the two characteristics work together to justify Paul's repetition as beneficial rather than burdensome.

The characteristic is named 'Indolence' in the programme (Hebrew shiphlut, H8220). The name signals a sinking/lowering quality -- inactivity that results in structural decay, essential nature tied to neglect producing physical deterioration.

H8220 shows at the definitional level 'sinking, idleness, inactivity' -- a noun capturing both the literal sense of sinking/collapsing and the metaphorical sense of slack hands/idleness leading to that collapse.

The name carries a constitutional implication: indolence is not merely absence of work but a cause producing tangible ruin (the house leaks, the roof sinks) -- implying a direct causal/relational link between neglect and structural failure.

Primary Hebrew term is shiphlut (H8220), a construct-form noun. Root meaning shows 'sinking, idleness, inactivity' -- likely related to the root for lowness/sinking (shaphel), tying idleness conceptually to a downward, collapsing motion.

The vocabulary arc for H8220 is narrow -- a single gloss cluster ('sinking, idleness, inactivity'), showing the term's complete semantic range is confined to this one hapax-like occurrence in Eccl.10.18, paired poetically with H6103 (sloth) in synonymous parallelism.

This occurrence sits within the base gloss with no notable divergence -- 'indolence' causing the house to leak matches the sinking/inactivity sense directly; this is effectively the term's sole/defining occurrence.

H8220 is grammatically a noun (feminine singular construct, HNcfsc), showing the characteristic operates as an abstract condition/state-noun describing a quality of hands/persons rather than an action itself.

The semantic range of H8220 spans literal sinking/lowering and metaphorical idleness/inactivity; in Eccl.10.18 it operates idiomatically in construct with 'hands' (H3027G, yadayim) — 'through indolence of hands' — implying that slack, low-hanging hands cause the house's structural collapse, a vivid analogical link between bodily posture and neglect.

The vocabulary here does distinguish disposition versus act: H6103 (sloth/sluggishness, a disposition) and H8220 (indolence, tied to slack hands, closer to a condition/state of inactivity) appear in parallel, distinguishing a general lazy disposition from a specific condition of idle hands.

none -- no structural-opposite term (e.g. diligence) is present in this verse's own vocabulary for H8220, though the cluster's own H0629 (diligence) elsewhere in the cluster serves that structural-opposite role.
none -- no distinct person-type term (e.g. 'the indolent one') is attested for H8220 in the given sources.
none -- no supplication/seeking term is attested for indolence.

H8220 has no direct NT Greek counterpart in this cluster's data; its conceptual opposite pairing runs instead with G0692 (argos, idle) which continues the idleness theme into the NT, showing continuity of the idleness/inactivity concept across Testaments even without shared root vocabulary.
none -- H8220 is an OT Hebrew term; NT coinage question does not apply.

Eccl.10.18 also carries M24 (H6103, sloth) and M23/M72 (H3027G, hand). From indolence's own vantage: H8220 supplies the causal/resultative link -- it names the condition (slack-handed idleness) that translates the disposition of sloth (M24) into the physical outcome via the hand (M23/M72), i.e. indolence is the mechanism connecting sloth-as-disposition to hand-as-instrument, producing the house's collapse. No prior cluster context exists for this verse.

Matt.20.3 has role-T3 operation words G1831 (going out), G2476 (standing). G0692 (idle) is an adjective describing the state of 'others' (the party) found standing in the marketplace -- it does not itself initiate an operation but characterizes the party's condition as the object of the householder's seeing/going-out action, directed toward them.
The characteristic is named 'Idleness' in the programme (Greek argos, G0692, from a-ergos 'not-working'). The name signals inactivity/unemployment as its essential nature, literally 'without work'.

Greek argos shows at the definitional level 'idle, lazy; useless, ineffective; careless' (Mounce), with LSJ confirming the etymology (a-ergos, contracted aergos) meaning 'not working the ground', 'idle, lazy', extending to 'unwrought, unprepared, unpolished' for things and 'not done, left undone' for actions.

The name carries a relational implication of unemployment/unengagement: in Matt.20.3 argos describes laborers standing in the marketplace awaiting an employer, implying a state of waiting to be engaged rather than culpable laziness -- a directional 'not-yet-directed' status.

Primary Greek term is argos (G0692), from a- privative + ergon 'work'. Root meaning shows 'not working', extended to idle/lazy/inactive, and by extension useless/ineffective/careless when applied metaphorically to speech or fruit (2Pet.1.8, Matt.12.36).

The full vocabulary arc of argos ranges from literal 'not working the ground/unemployed' (Matt.20.3,6) through moral 'lazy, averse from labor' (1Tim.5.13, Titus.1.12) to metaphorical 'unfruitful/ineffective' (2Pet.1.8) and 'careless, useless' of words/deeds (Matt.12.36, Jas.2.20), and even technical senses like 'lying fallow' (land) or 'yielding no return' (money) in Classical Greek -- showing a semantic range from physical inactivity to moral and metaphorical unproductiveness.

In Matt.20.3 argos describes day-laborers standing unemployed in the marketplace, sitting within the base gloss 'idle, unemployed' with a neutral/circumstantial nuance (lack of work opportunity) rather than the morally-loaded 'lazy, careless' sense found in 1Tim.5.13/Titus.1.12/Jas.2.20. The impact here is descriptive of economic circumstance, not moral censure, contrasting with other occurrences where argos implies culpable inactivity or uselessness.

G0692 is grammatically an adjective (A-APM here, accusative plural masculine), showing the characteristic operates as a descriptive quality attributed to persons or things (people, land, money, words) rather than as a verb or noun in its own right.

The semantic range of argos spans literal non-labor (unemployed persons), disuse of land/money ('lying fallow', 'yielding no return'), and metaphorical unfruitfulness of faith/words (2Pet.1.8, Matt.12.36) -- in combination with genitive objects it can mean 'idle at/free from' a thing (e.g. 'slow to evil'), showing an idiomatic breadth beyond simple laziness.

The vocabulary here distinguishes condition versus quality: in Matt.20.3 argos describes a temporary condition (unemployed at this hour, standing idle awaiting hire) rather than a fixed moral quality of laziness, contrasting with its use in 1Tim.5.13/Titus.1.12 where it denotes an ingrained habitual quality.
The structural opposite is present in this cluster's own vocabulary: G4710 (spoude, haste/zeal/diligence), directly contrasting argos's inactivity with eager engagement/effort.
none -- no distinct person-type term (beyond the adjective itself substantivally applied, e.g. 'the idle ones') is attested for argos in the given sources.
none -- no supplication/seeking term for idleness is attested.

G0692 (argos) parallels the OT idleness vocabulary (H6103 sloth, H8220 indolence in Eccl.10.18) showing continuity of the idleness concept across Testaments; the NT usage extends the concept metaphorically into moral/spiritual unfruitfulness (2Pet.1.8, Jas.2.20) beyond the OT's largely domestic/physical framing (roof sinking, house leaking).
none -- argos is a well-attested Classical Greek term (Herodotus, Sophocles, Aristotle, etc.), not a NT coinage.

Matt.20.3 also carries M15 (G1492H, saw) alongside G0692. From idleness's own vantage: the idleness of 'others' is precisely the state that the M15 seeing-action discovers/targets -- G0692 supplies the object-condition that motivates the householder's seeing and subsequent action (hiring), i.e. idleness is what is perceived. No prior cluster context exists for this verse.

G1492H (eidon/oida, 'saw'/'know') is not this cluster's own characteristic but is front-loaded here. Its name signals perceptive knowledge -- the verb 'to see' functioning also as 'to know', reflecting the ancient conceptual link between visual perception and cognitive knowledge.

Primary Greek term is eidon (aorist of horao)/oida (perfect-as-present), root eido/video family. Root meanings show 'to see, perceive, behold' (aorist) and 'to know, have knowledge of' (perfect), reflecting the Indo-European root shared with Latin videre and Sanskrit veda 'to know'.

H3027G (yad, 'hand') is not this cluster's own characteristic but is front-loaded here. Its name signals the instrument/agent of human action and power -- the hand as the primary organ of doing, and by extension of strength and possession.

Primary Hebrew term is yad (H3027G). Root meaning shows 'hand (of man)' with figurative extension to 'strength, power', 'side, part, portion', and various technical senses (sign/monument, share, time/repetition, axle-trees, tenons, wrists) -- a highly productive body-part term used broadly for agency and power.

H6103 (sloth) is not this cluster's own characteristic but is front-loaded here. Its name signals sluggishness/laziness as a disposition -- distinct from H8220's condition-focus, this term names the habitual character trait itself.

Primary Hebrew term is atslah (H6103, plural form here). Root meaning shows 'sluggishness, laziness' -- from the same root family as atsel (sluggard), naming the general disposition of habitual laziness paired in this verse with H8220's more specific idle-hands condition.

The characteristic is 'thanksgiving/praise' (yadah), named from a root meaning 'to throw/cast' extended to the act of casting forth words of acknowledgment toward another -- an act oriented outward, publicly declaring gratitude or confession rather than a purely internal disposition.

The characteristic is 'seeking/inquiring' (darash in Hebrew), naming a devotional and investigative pursuit -- especially seeking God through worship, prayer, or consultation.

Darash at the definitional level shows resorting to/frequenting a place, consulting or inquiring of (especially God or oracles), seeking deity in prayer and worship, demanding/requiring, investigating, and practicing/studying with application -- a term centered on devotional and investigative pursuit rather than mere physical search.

Verb occurring in Qal (active seeking) and Niphal (passive, be sought/be enquired of by God, or be required as of blood), showing the term functions both as human devotional action and as a divine self-disclosure/response category.

No prior context recorded. In Amos.5.14 darash co-occurs with M05/M18 (good), M24/M58 (evil), M25 (live); this characteristic's vantage adds that seeking is the verb governing the moral choice between the two named opposites (good vs evil), making it the pivot-action of the verse.

No prior context recorded. The characteristic is 'Seek/Search' (bāqaš, Piel). The name signals purposeful, directed pursuit toward finding or securing an object, person, or divine presence, not aimless wandering.

In Prov.17.11 the same Piel verb bāqaš names the evil man's habitual pursuit of rebellion, showing the term's neutral capacity to be directed at either good (seeking the Lord) or evil (seeking rebellion) objects.

Hebrew bāqaš (Piel) shows at the definitional level: to seek to find, seek to secure, seek the face of, demand, require, or request. Every sense involves active, intentional pursuit of an object not yet possessed or present.

The name carries a directional implication: motion of the will toward an object (the Lord, David, rebellion), and a relational implication when the object is a person -- seeking the Lord's face implies covenantal return and restored relationship (Hos.3.5).

Primary Hebrew term is bāqaš (H1245); its root meaning centers on active seeking/searching with intent to find or secure, extending to formal 'seeking the face' of God and to 'requiring/demanding' in legal or relational contexts.

Grammatical range is verbal only (Piel/Pual stems attested), showing the characteristic operates purely as an action/process rather than a static quality -- it is something one does, not something one has.

Semantic range spans from concrete search (locate a lost object/person) to relational pursuit ('seek the Lord's face') to legal/economic demand (exact, require) to simple request. In Hos.3.5 the idiom 'seek the Lord' carries covenantal-return sense; in Prov.17.11 it carries habitual-disposition sense (seeking rebellion as a lifestyle).

No distinct vocabulary terms within bāqaš itself split disposition versus act or received versus given; the single verb covers both the momentary act and (via participial/habitual use) an implied disposition.
No structural-opposite term is supplied among the meaning sources for bāqaš; 'not seeking' or forsaking would be expressed by separate distinct roots not present here.
No dedicated person-type noun ('seeker') is given among the sources for bāqaš in these verses; the participial usage functions descriptively rather than as a fixed agent-noun.
No separate supplication term is distinguished from bāqaš itself; the sense 'to ask, request' (1a6) already covers the supplication nuance within the same lemma.

The OT bāqaš and NT Greek zēteō/epizēteō show strong continuity: both denote purposeful seeking that can be directed at God, a sign, or a person, and both carry the idiom of 'seeking someone's life' to mean seeking to kill (paralleling Prov.17.11's cruel-pursuit sense and Matt.2.20's zēteō tēn psychēn).
bāqaš is a well-established pre-NT Hebrew root, attested widely across the Hebrew Bible; not a coinage question (Hebrew, not Greek NT period).

The full vocabulary arc of bāqaš ranges from finding a lost object, to seeking a person's favor, to seeking God's face in covenant restoration, to seeking to secure or exact something owed, to seeking someone's harm (via idiom) -- showing the term's range is defined entirely by its object, not by any internal semantic split.
In Hos.3.5 bāqaš is used in its central sense of seeking God/covenant restoration, squarely within the base gloss; no notable divergence from ordinary usage.

In Prov.17.11 bāqaš is used of an evil man's habitual pursuit of rebellion; this sits within the base gloss's 'desire, demand' sense (a negative object rather than a divergent form), so no surface-form shift is present -- the negativity comes from the object 'rebellion', not from the verb's own nuance.

In Hos.3.5, bāqaš (seek) co-occurs with H6342 (fear) and other M-coded terms (H1732 David/king M72, H0430 God/Lord T10/T7) but these are role-classification tags (T-codes) not M-codes with home membership here; among genuine M-code characteristics present, seeking the Lord functions as the initiating disposition that precedes and enables the subsequent 'fear/awe' response toward the Lord and his goodness -- the two are sequential rather than overlapping in this verse's own action.

In Prov.17.11, bāqaš (seek) co-occurs with M24/M58 (evil man) and M30 (rebellion) and M10 (cruel messenger); the seeking here is the operative link between the evil disposition (M24/M58) and its object (rebellion, M30) -- the evil man's character finds active expression through the act of seeking, while the cruel messenger (M10) is the resulting consequence, not something seeking itself connects to directly.

H1245 (seek) is not tagged role-T3 in either Hos.3.5 or Prov.17.11 in the role list provided (it carries only M83); the role-T3 operation tags in these verses belong to other strongs (H7725 return, H7971 sent), so D7.7.1 does not apply to this home strong directly in these verses.
The characteristic is 'Seek/Look for' (zēteō). The name signals active pursuit -- physically searching, intellectually inquiring, or volitionally desiring -- toward an object not currently possessed.

The name carries a directional implication (motion of will/action toward an object) and, in hostile contexts (Herod seeking the child, seeking the child's life), a relational implication of threat directed at a person.
zēteō is attested extensively in classical Greek (Herodotus, Plato, Xenophon, Sophocles) well before the NT period; not a NT coinage.

The full vocabulary arc of zēteō spans physical searching, crowd-seeking for a person, hostile seeking-to-kill, seeking a confirming sign, demonic seeking of rest, and imperative seeking commanded of disciples -- showing the term's range is set entirely by its grammatical subject and object rather than by internal lexical splits.

In Matt.2.13 'search for the child, to destroy him' zēteō carries its plain physical-search sense reinforced by the following purpose infinitive apolesai (destroy); no divergence within the verb itself beyond its ordinary range.

In Matt.2.13, zēteō (search) co-occurs with M10 (destroy/apollymi); the search here functions as the preparatory operation whose completion enables the destructive act -- zēteō names the investigative means, M10 names the intended lethal end.

In Matt.2.13, zēteō is tagged role-T3 (operation) with Herod as the initiating party, directed toward the child (party present as object); the angel's prior command to flee frames this search as a hostile pursuit to be evaded.

The characteristic is 'Seek for/demand' (epizēteō), an intensive compound of zēteō. The prefix epi- signals an added intensity or directedness -- seeking after, wishing for, or missing something, often with a demanding edge.
Greek epizēteō shows at the definitional level: seek after, wish for, miss, require, demand, inquire further -- an intensified variant of the base seeking-family idea.

The name carries a directional-demanding implication: the generation's seeking is directed at Jesus, demanding a sign as proof, implying a relational posture of testing/unbelief rather than trustful request.
Primary Greek term epizēteō (G1934), a compound of epi + zēteō; root meaning intensifies the base 'seek' into 'seek after, demand, require' with added urgency or fixation on the object.
Grammatical range is verbal only (present indicative in both occurrences here), consistent with the term's function as ongoing habitual action attributed to 'this generation.'

Semantic range includes seeking/wishing for, missing something absent, requiring/demanding, and (in Koine legal/papyrus use) formal request; in the Gospels it is consistently used of demanding a confirming sign, carrying a testing/unbelieving connotation.
No internal vocabulary split within epizēteō distinguishes disposition from act; both occurrences here are the same act-type present-tense usage describing a generation's characteristic demand.
No structural opposite term is supplied for epizēteō among the sources.
No dedicated person-type agent noun for epizēteō is given among the sources.
No distinct supplication term separate from epizēteō is present in these verses; the term's own 'demand' sense already covers the request nuance.

As a NT-period intensified compound of the seek-family, epizēteō shows continuity with Hebrew dāraš/bāqaš in the sense of demanding proof/inquiry, while its heightened form reflects Koine tendency to intensify simple verbs by compounding with prepositions.

epizēteō is attested in classical and Hellenistic Greek (Herodotus, Demosthenes, Polybius, papyri) well before the NT; not a NT coinage, though its NT usage narrows toward the specific idiom of demanding a sign.

The full vocabulary arc of epizēteō in the NT is narrower than zēteō, concentrated on demanding a sign from Jesus as proof, showing a specialized rhetorical use of the intensive compound for a specific recurring controversy scene.
In Matt.12.39 epizēteō carries its established Gospel sense of demanding a sign; matches the term's consistent usage elsewhere (e.g. Luke.11.29), no additional divergence.
In Luke.11.29 epizēteō repeats the identical idiom and sense found in Matt.12.39 (demanding a sign from 'this generation'), showing no divergence between occurrences.

In Luke.11.29, epizēteō (seeks for) co-occurs with M08 (began), M58 (evil), and M43 (sign, x3); as in Matt.12.39, the evil characterization of the generation supplies the moral cause of its sign-demanding act, with epizēteō serving as the link-verb between disposition and demanded object.
In Matt.12.39, epizēteō is role-T3, initiated by 'an evil and adulterous generation' and directed at Jesus (the implicit addressee 'he answered them') demanding a sign.
In Luke.11.29, epizēteō is role-T3, initiated by 'this generation' and directed at Jesus, demanding a sign as in the parallel Matt.12.39 saying.

Primary Greek term: ekzēteō (G1567), from ek + zēteō. Root meaning: intensive/exhaustive seeking, seeking out, or demanding/requiring an account. The vocabulary distinguishes intensive/exhaustive seeking (ekzēteō) from ordinary seeking (zēteō, its base form) -- an act-versus-degree-of-act distinction, where ek- marks completeness/thoroughness of the searching act rather than a disposition.

No structural opposite or absence-term for ekzēteō is present among the three sources; the concept's negation would be expressed periphrastically (e.g. failing to seek) rather than by a distinct lexeme.
No distinct person-type noun (e.g. 'seeker') is attested for ekzēteō in these sources; the word remains verbal throughout its NT and classical attestations.

Ekzēteō itself carries a supplication sense in one of its own uses (Heb 12:17, 'to ask for, beseech earnestly'), meaning the same lexeme doubles as the 'seeking from another' term rather than requiring a separate supplication word.

BC papyri, Josephus) and its judicial 'demand an account of' sense already present in the LXX (2 Kings/2 Sam 4:11), showing continuity of the Hebraic idiom of blood being 'sought/required' carried directly into NT Greek usage (Luke.11.50-51) rather than being a new coinage.
Ekzēteō is not a NT coinage; LSJ documents it in 1st century BC papyri and other Hellenistic sources prior to and contemporary with the NT.

Primary Greek term: zēteō (G2212). Root meaning per LSJ: 'seek, seek for, search after, inquire, investigate, desire, require, demand.' No Hebrew primary term supplied in these sources, though the sense overlaps with baqash/darash word-fields for seeking in the OT.
In John.1.38 'What are you seeking?' is a direct, literal use of zēteō asking about the disciples' immediate purpose -- within the base gloss, no shift.

In John.11.56 'looking for Jesus' at the feast is a neutral searching-for-a-person sense, without hostile or ironic shading -- within the base gloss.
No distinct person-type noun ('seeker') is attested for zēteō among these sources; the concept remains expressed verbally throughout.

In John.11.56 M15 (dokeō, 'think') co-occurs with M83 (zēteō, 'looking for'). From M83's vantage, the crowd's active searching for Jesus is distinct from their separate act of opining/speculating (M15) about whether he will come -- the seeking is physical/locational while the thinking is deliberative, running in parallel rather than intersecting.
The word dokeō names 'to think, consider, regard, seem' -- an operation of the mind processing information into judgment or opinion, often used impersonally ('it seems').

Primary Greek term: dokeō (G1380). Root meaning per LSJ: 'expect, suppose, seem, be reputed,' with an original sense tied to δέχομαι-cognates of receiving/forming an impression. No Hebrew term supplied.

H1245 (baqash) is this cluster's home term for 'seeking' -- the programme names it as the disposition/act of actively pursuing something desired or required, including seeking God, seeking help, or seeking sustenance. Its essential nature is directed pursuit, not passive hope.

H1245 at the definitional level denotes active seeking-to-find or seeking-to-secure, including seeking a person's face, demanding, requesting; the Piel stem intensifies the pursuit as deliberate effort rather than chance encounter.

The name carries a strongly directional/relational implication: it always assumes an object sought (water, food, God, a person) and implies a relationship of pursuit toward that object, often with the further implication of a response awaited from what is sought.

H1245's Piel root meanings converge on active, applied seeking: to seek to find, to seek to secure, to seek a face, to desire/demand, to require/exact, to ask/request; Pual passive 'to be sought' extends the range to the object's being pursued by another.

H1245 occurs as a verb across Piel active participle (seeking, ongoing action, Isa.41.17, Exod.33.7), Piel perfect (completed seeking, Hos.7.10, Lam.1.19), and Pual passive (seek/be sought, 2Chr.7.14) -- showing the characteristic operates primarily as an ongoing or repeated action rather than a static state.

H1245's semantic range spans physical seeking (water, food -- Isa.41.17, Lam.1.19), covenantal/cultic seeking (seeking the LORD at the tent of meeting, seeking his face -- Exod.33.7, 2Chr.7.14), and idiomatic non-return (Hos.7.10, negated seeking as covenant failure); it can combine with 'face' (H6440) idiomatically to mean seek audience/favor with someone.

No distinct vocabulary within H1245's own forms differentiates disposition-versus-act or received-versus-given; the Piel/Pual distinction is grammatical voice (active seeking vs being sought), not a disposition/act split.

H1245 has no lexically distinct structural opposite within this cluster's own vocabulary; the contrast in these verses is expressed by separate verbs (e.g. H5800A 'forsake') rather than a dedicated antonym of 'seek' itself.

No dedicated person-type noun (e.g. 'seeker') derives from H1245 in these occurrences; the participle functions attributively of 'the poor and needy' or 'everyone' rather than naming a fixed class-title.

H1245 itself functions as the supplication/seeking term for this cluster -- the act of seeking something (including God) from another is precisely its core sense, most explicit in 2Chr.7.14's seeking God's face as a penitential act.

As an OT Hebrew term, H1245 establishes seeking-God as covenantal practice (tent of meeting, temple prayer); this pattern anticipates NT-period seeking language (e.g. Greek zeteo) that carries forward the same directed-pursuit sense toward God -- continuity of concept across Testaments, though this cluster's own NT term is not covered by these front-loaded strongs.
H1245 is an OT Hebrew term well attested across the Hebrew Bible pre-dating the NT period entirely; no coinage question applies to the Hebrew term itself.

Across its five occurrences here H1245 spans the full arc from desperate physical need (water/food) through covenantal reform (turning, humbling, seeking face) to prophetic indictment (failure to seek despite testimony) -- showing the characteristic's range runs from bodily survival-seeking to the highest register of covenant relationship-seeking.
In Isa.41.17 'seek' (participle, ongoing) sits squarely within H1245's base gloss of active pursuit of water; no divergent nuance beyond the standard sense of seeking a needed resource.

The characteristic is 'Seeking' (G2212 zeteo). The name signals an active, purposeful pursuit — to look for, search out, or strive to obtain something not yet possessed, whether concrete (a person) or abstract (truth, righteousness, God).

Primary Hebrew term baqash (Piel/Pual); root meaning centers on intentional seeking-to-find or seeking-to-secure, extending to requesting/demanding from a superior or seeking a person's favor.

The characteristic is named for the Hebrew darash, 'to seek/enquire/require' -- signalling an essential nature of active, purposeful pursuit rather than passive reception; the name marks seeking as a deliberate directed act toward God, counsel, or things demanding investigation.

At the definitional level darash covers resorting to a place, consulting/enquiring (of God or diviners), seeking deity in prayer and worship, demanding/requiring, investigating, and studying/practicing with application -- a term whose core is deliberate, engaged pursuit, not casual looking.

The name carries a strongly relational and directional implication: seeking is always toward an object -- most often God -- implying covenant orientation, dependence, and the expectation of a response (being 'found' or 'enquired of').

Grammatical range is verbal only (Qal and Niphal), appearing as finite verbs, infinitives, and participles across these verses -- showing the characteristic operates as an action performed by an agent, never as an abstract noun-state in this strong.

Semantic range spans literal enquiry (questioning priests about heaps, 2Chr.31.9), legal/covenant seeking of God through commandments (Ps.119.2,10; 2Chr.17.4; 31.21), and requiring/consulting objects like the ark (1Chr.13.3) -- showing an idiomatic extension from physical resort to spiritual devotion.
